newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline catches its breath.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Products Outlook - Gasoline catches its breath.

text.p: Gasoline prices east of the Rocky Mountains look likely to pause this week after a sharp bounce in the previous two weeks, traders said.

But they did say ingredients that have fueled gasoline, including heavy speculator interest, solid summer demand, and a spiking market for the key gasoline additive methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), are still factors in the market.
"For the next three weeks, things will continue to be constructive," said one trader, noting relief in the form of big imports will not come before the second week of August.

But some sources said historical price patterns loom bearishly over last week's spike that saw the bellwether "M1," regular unleaded, grade for prompt delivery in Houston rise by nearly seven percent to nearly 60 cents a gallon.

Some traders and analysts said that, notwithstanding the drama surrounding one Gulf Coast trader's short position last week, demand has probably peaked and prices are likely to soon begin a sustained descent that could last into the coming winter.

"Is production still at high levels? Is the Fourth of July over? Do we have enough gasoline to make it through summer?," asked one trader rhetorically, noting that the typical seasonal rally usually runs out of steam by mid-July.
U.S GULF COAST

Last week's M1 fireworks sparked by one trader's frenetic activity to cover short commitments to a number of other trade players, particularly a major Wall Street player, gave way this week to a lull amid talk those commitments are now covered.
"I think the people who covered did it last week, and they had to have it done by Friday," said one Gulf Coast trader.
Indeed cash differentials on prompt M1 on Friday got as firm as 2.25 cents over August NYMEX unleaded before settling back to about 0.60 cent over by the end of the day.
The new prompt M1 for delivery by Colonial Pipeline's front 21st cycle scheduling deadline on Thursday were even weaker at between 0.75 and 0.50 cent under the August print.
Still, traders were taking a wait-and-see attitude to see if the recent tightness in Houston gasoline markets again rears its head at the next Colonial shipping deadline.
"There's no scheduling deadline (for M1) until July 17th so between now and then we'll see who's for real," the Gulf trader said.

Traders said tightness remains in the Gulf Coast market, fueled by good demand at the pump and by MTBE's recent price spike, which is making blending reformulated gasoline more expensive, thus contributing to tightness.
"It may not get as strong as it has been, but I still think it's going to be tight," said another Gulf Coast trader.
"MTBE is rocking and it continues to rock. Blending doesn't work," he added. MTBE is used to raise oxygen required in reformulated fuels, and to raise octane levels.

Some players suggested some of the gasoline cargoes scheduled to arrive on the East Coast during the first 10 days of August may be diverted to the Southeast to help ease the tightness in Gulf Coast gasoline markets.
NEW YORK HARBOR
The effects of MTBE's strength, which is linked to maintenance activity in late spring that left the market thirsty for more barrels than expected, was helping premium gasoline blends in the Harbor.
The "D2" 93-octane premium reformulated blend traded at firmer levels Monday morning at 8.75 cents over August NYMEX, showing that last week's strength was still alive.
The "V2" conventional 93-octane premium was also holding its gains from last week.
But overall, the market was characterized by divergent views, and like in Houston, waiting for a better read on the uncertain road ahead.
"It's been pretty quiet so far today. I don't think the Harbor's very tight."

Some market watchers said gasoline imports from Europe were fixed last week during a brief period when U.S. premiums reached levels high enough to make shipments economic, though shipping fixtures for end-July/early August couldn't be confirmed.
Most players were in agreement, however, that cargoes should start arriving in greater numbers by early August.
MIDCONTINENT
Action in the midcontinent was in profit-taking mode.
A gasoline sell-off was largely spurred by the decline in U.S. Gulf Coast differentials and the drop in NYMEX futures following Iraqi news.
"We are coming off last week's strength and sellers want to catch what premium is left for the prompt values," said one Group Three trader.
